articles.title: Coreia do Sul analisa obrigar mulheres a servir no Exército | G1
articles.standfirst: Declínio populacional, redução de recrutas e apoio da sociedade pode levar coreanos a quebrarem o tabu que impede o gênero feminino na linha de frente. Tecnologia, no entanto, é mais urgente.
articles.summary: Declínio populacional, redução de recrutas e apoio da sociedade pode levar coreanos a quebrarem o tabu que impede o gênero feminino na linha de frente.
articles.body:
Forças Armadas da Coreia do Sul enfrentam escassez de pessoal, que deve ser foco de reforma do governo — Foto: Xinhua/IMAGO via DW

Quase 60% dos sul-coreanos se declaram a favor de que jovens mulheres cumpram o serviço militar obrigatório ao lado dos colegas do sexo masculino , de acordo com uma pesquisa recente, o que representa uma mudança significativa no tabu de longa data contra a obrigação delas de defender a nação.

Milhares de pessoas do sexo feminino já servem nas Forças Armadas da Coreia do Sul de forma voluntária, mas o debate sobre o serviço obrigatório sempre foi delicado.

Agora, por uma série de razões que incluem queda na taxa de natalidade e redução no número de recrutas, além de uma insistência de que a igualdade social implica que as mulheres também devam servir nas Forças Armadas, a questão voltou à tona antes de uma reforma do plano de defesa nacional, cuja divulgação está prevista para este segundo semestre.

No entanto, ainda há quem insista que as mulheres devam ser mantidas longe da linha de frente e que, em vez disso, a Coreia do Sul deva investir mais em drones e outras tecnologias avançadas.

"O sistema de alistamento militar da Coreia do Sul, focado nos homens, está há muito tempo intimamente ligado aos papéis tradicionais de gênero", afirma Hyobin Lee, professora da Universidade Sogang, em Seul.

"Em geral, esperava-se que os homens protegessem o país e a família e lutassem em tempos de guerra, enquanto as mulheres assumiam a responsabilidade principal pelo parto, pelos cuidados com os filhos e pelas tarefas domésticas", diz ela à DW.

Um segundo fator é o debate cada vez mais acirrado sobre a igualdade de gênero, um impulsionado em grande parte por jovens do sexo masculino, acrescenta Hyobin Lee.

Como conta Lee, os homens sul-coreanos geralmente cumprem o serviço militar no início dos 20 anos, o que os obriga a interromper estudos, emprego ou desenvolvimento inicial das carreiras deles.

"Ao mesmo tempo, a igualdade de gênero tornou-se um valor social cada vez mais importante, e as oportunidades das mulheres na educação e no mercado de trabalho se ampliaram", explica a pesquisadora.

"Como resultado, alguns homens mais jovens fazem uma pergunta muito simples: se a sociedade espera igualdade de direitos e oportunidades, por que uma das obrigações cívicas mais significativas do país – o serviço militar – ainda recai apenas sobre os homens?"

Outro fator que contribui para isso é a mudança na própria natureza das Forças Armadas, com um afastamento das funções de combate fisicamente mais exigentes, que eram vistas como mais adequadas aos homens, e o surgimento de uma defesa nacional que depende cada vez mais da tecnologia.

Isso inclui sistemas não tripulados, capacidades cibernéticas, tecnologia da informação e comunicação e outros que não exigem força física.

Veículos blindados dos EUA em exercício de travessia de rio próximo à Coreia do Norte — Foto: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance via DW

De acordo com o estudo, realizado pelo Reform Institute, o braço de pesquisa política do Partido da Reforma, de tendência conservadora, e publicado em 20 de agosto, quase 60% dos entrevistados se mostraram a favor de alterar a lei para exigir que as mulheres prestem serviço nacional. Apenas 34% se opuseram à ideia.

Quase 65% dos homens eram a favor – parcela que subiu para 71,7% entre os homens na faixa dos 20 e 30 anos –, enquanto 54,5% das mulheres, em todas as faixas etárias, também se mostraram favoráveis.

Atualmente, todos os homens fisicamente aptos são obrigados a cumprir um período mínimo de 18 meses e máximo de 21 meses de serviço e podem ser convocados novamente em caso de emergência nacional, como o início de uma guerra na tensa Península Coreana.

Os números mais recentes destacam, no entanto, a escassez de pessoal que as Forças Armadas da Coreia do Sul estão enfrentando.

De acordo com o Ministério da Defesa, cerca de 332 mil homens estavam aptos a cumprir o serviço militar obrigatório em 2019, mas esse número caiu para 257 mil em 2022 e deve diminuir para apenas 120 mil em 2043.

No entanto, Lee teme que obrigar as mulheres a cumprir o mesmo período de serviço militar que os homens possa acabar tendo efeitos negativos, já que muitos outros aspectos da sociedade ainda apresentam atrasos.

Responsabilidade das mulheres continua igual

Torre de observação sul-coreana na fronteira com a Coreia do Norte — Foto: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance via DW

De acordo com a pesquisadora, as mulheres na Coreia do Sul ainda arcam com uma parcela muito maior das responsabilidades associadas à gravidez, ao parto e aos cuidados com os filhos.

"Ter um filho ainda pode levar à interrupção da carreira ou à saída do mercado de trabalho, e as responsabilidades das mulheres com os cuidados familiares não diminuíram na mesma proporção em que aumentou sua participação na educação e no emprego", acrescenta Lee.

"Se as mulheres também fossem obrigadas a cumprir o serviço militar, a carga acumulada ao longo de suas vidas poderia se tornar ainda maior."

Em um país que já enfrenta uma taxa de natalidade extremamente baixa, também é possível que essa obrigação a mais possa adiar ainda mais ou desestimular o casamento e a maternidade, diz.

Lee vem de uma família com forte tradição militar: o avô dela foi almirante da Marinha e o pai serviu no mesmo ramo das Forças Armadas.

Mas ela mesma teria reservas em cumprir o serviço militar obrigatório.

"Se alguém opta por uma carreira militar, isso é completamente diferente do serviço militar obrigatório", pontua. "Dezoito meses na casa dos 20 anos é um período muito significativo na vida de uma pessoa. É uma época em que as pessoas estão estudando, iniciando a carreira e tomando decisões pessoais importantes. Ter que colocar tudo isso em espera porque o Estado exige é um fardo considerável."

"Pessoalmente, eu teria achado extremamente difícil abrir mão de 18 meses da minha juventude dessa maneira", admite a pesquisadora.

Song Young-Chae, acadêmico e ativista de direitos humanos que mora em Seul, cumpriu dois anos na infantaria quando era mais jovem, época em que os períodos de serviço eram mais longos, e se opõe ao serviço militar obrigatório para as mulheres.

"A defesa da nação é, tradicionalmente, responsabilidade dos homens, e não acredito que haja uma necessidade tão urgente de alistar mulheres para o serviço na linha de frente", diz ele à DW.

Song serviu na Zona Desmilitarizada (DMZ), na fronteira com a Coreia do Norte. "Foi uma missão difícil", conta ele, que acredita que o mais importante, no mometo, é investir em drones, robôs e outras tecnologias militares avançadas para proteger as fronteiras do país asiático.

O governo sul-coreano criou uma força-tarefa no ano passado para revisar o plano básico de defesa do país, tendo como prioridades a modernização das tropas e uma reforma do sistema de alistamento obrigatório – introduzido na década de 1950.

Em entrevista à Yonhap News, a comissária de Recursos Humanos Militares, Hong So-young, admitiu que o país enfrenta um "abismo demográfico" e que são necessárias reformas urgentes, incluindo a possível redução do número de pessoas isentas do serviço militar e a exigência de que pessoas nascidas no exterior que tenham adquirido a nacionalidade sul-coreana também prestem serviço.

A comissária não fez comentários na entrevista de 9 de agosto sobre o serviço militar obrigatório para mulheres coreanas, mas afirmou que o sistema precisa de uma reforma "fundamental".

articles.title: Couple recounts surviving deadly Nepal flood: "I knew I was going to die"
articles.summary: A California couple were in a Nepali village when an avalanche of powerful waters ripped down from the high Himalayas toward them.
articles.body:
A couple from the San Francisco Bay Area who were on a pilgrimage to Tibet told CBS News on Friday that they thought they were going to die when they saw a mountain of water coming toward them earlier this week.

"I knew I was going to die," Anjana Raja told CBS News. "I knew I was going to die."

The catastrophic flash flooding that struck a mountainous border area of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday — when a glacier in the Himalayas collapsed and sent torrents of water into the valleys below — has killed nearly 600 people, with an estimated 2,500 more believed to be missing as search and rescue crews frantically scour for survivors.

The U.S. State Department said Friday that about 90 Americans are estimated to be among the missing.

When the avalanche of powerful waters ripped down from the high Himalayas, the melting glacier and debris first hit the Nepali village of Timure, near where Raja and her partner Pattabiraman Venkatesan were with their tour bus.

The couple were making their first pilgrimage to Tibet, an autonomous region of China that shares a border with Nepal. They had driven through Timure, and were in the bus in Nepal's Rasuwa District, near the Nepal-China border, when what looked like a tsunami appeared.

"It's like 60, 70 feet, it looked like a tsunami, but dark black," Venkatesan said. "... I could see this monster thing coming down. At that point I didn't know if it was water. I thought it was fire, forest fire, honestly."

Raja said she grabbed Venkatesan by the collar, pulled him and said, "Run," as the two of them jumped off the bus.

As thousands of people ran for their lives, cellphone videos showed some getting swallowed into the churn, while others were able to climb to safety higher up and were eventually airlifted out.

The couple said they sprinted up a set of steps trying to reach higher ground.

"Along the way, you know, houses were coming down, it was bringing down homes," Venkatesan said.

Raja said she could hear the screams of people who were being swept away by the floodwaters below.

"I saw death right in front of my eyes," Raja said.

A guide led them up to a flat area at the top of a nearby mountain. The climb was treacherous.

"So tall up, I don't know even how we climbed," Raja said. "It was really hard."

Venkatesan described the climb as "narrow and so slippery," with "mud and stones and rocks and everything."

They spent that night in a goat shed with several other survivors, including local residents and tourists, and were airlifted out the following day.

The couple said everyone aboard their tour bus survived.

"The fact that we survived is nothing short of a miracle," Venkatesan said.

The couple are counting their blessings. Venkatesan said the experience has given them a renewed appreciation for life.

"It strengthens my thought on life," Venkatesan said. "Be good, do good, think good, and leave the rest to whoever is above us. That's all I can say."

articles.title: Ecuador sentences ex-president Moreno to five years in jail in bribery case
articles.summary: Lenin Moreno, 73, has also been permanently barred from holding any public office in the future.
articles.body:
An Ecuadorian court has found former President Lenin Moreno guilty of bribery in a case tied to the construction of the country’s largest hydroelectric plant, the public prosecutor’s office said on Friday.

Moreno, 73, was sentenced to five years in prison and has been permanently barred from holding any public office in the future.

The attorney general’s office launched an investigation in March 2023, linking Moreno, his family members, and local and Chinese business partners to an alleged corruption network connected to the Coca Codo Sinclair plant . The facility began operating in 2016 and has experienced technical problems since.

“Lenin Moreno’s conduct is consistent with the charges brought by the prosecution: the crime of bribery attributed to a public official,” said Judge Manuel Cabrera, head of the tribunal, while delivering the ruling. The attorney general’s office said Chinese state-owned firm Sinohydro paid roughly $76.1m in bribes between 2009 and 2018 through fraudulent consulting contracts.

Moreno’s wife and daughter, along with his two brothers and their wives, were also convicted and sentenced to two and a half years in prison. Cai Runguo, China’s former ambassador to Quito, also received a five-year sentence.

Investigators alleged the funds moved through overseas accounts and shell companies in tax havens before reaching Moreno’s family and associates. Prosecutors said Moreno and his close relatives received more than $1m while he served as vice president from 2007 to 2013.

Moreno has consistently denied the allegations, insisting he had no role in signing or overseeing the project’s contracts.

“You’re looking in the wrong place. Look at those who signed the contracts, at those who had the habit of demanding kickbacks,” Moreno told the court during the hearing.

Moreno, who served as president from 2017 to 2021, returned to Ecuador from Paraguay to face trial.

articles.title: Missing toll from devastating floods in Nepal and China passes 3,000
articles.summary: Rescue efforts are in their fourth day but Nepali authorities are warning they are struggling to cope with the number of decomposing bodies recovered. Follow for news updates.
articles.body:
• Death toll: More than 600 people have been killed in Nepal and 7 have died in China following catastrophic flooding at the border . Officials are planning to bury unidentifiable bodies in a mass grave as authorities struggle to cope with the decomposing remains. Around 3,000 people are still missing both sides of the border.

• Flood fears: More rain is expected this weekend in flood-affected areas. Officials are closely monitoring two lakes , fueling fears of a new deluge.

• Scenes of devastation: Chinese state media reported there is no sign of survivors at a border crossing which was engulfed by the flood wave. And in Nepal, health officials said residents of a “whole village that seems to have been washed away” are in “dire need of support.”

• On the ground: CNN teams have witnessed devastated neighborhoods and families’ anguish while they desperately search for information on their missing relatives.

At Dhunge Bazaar after the rain had cleared — three JCB diggers resumed the painstaking task of reopening the road up to the China border where communities are still stranded following deadly landslides on Wednesday.

As of Saturday afternoon the diggers had cleared around 200 meters of the almost meter-high silt and mud, illustrating the enormity of the task of restoring communication to the hardest-hit areas up in the mountains.

The road — which winds through the hills for hours before reaching the China border — is Nepal’s main trade link with its giant northern neighbor.

A crowd of people gathered to watch the JCBs at work. Choppers flew overhead in a constant stream ferrying victims from a village just on the other side of the river.

Rescue teams in Nepal have located 187 tourists after deadly landslides ripped through the Himalayan nation on Wednesday, local officials said Saturday, with around 3,000 people still missing on both sides of the Nepal-China border.

Of those rescued, 114 are Indians, 27 are Chinese, and 20 are from South Korea, the US, Europe and the Gulf, according to a bulletin published by the Nepal Tourism Board.

At least 420 foreigners remain missing, the bulletin said.

The catastrophic torrents have killed more than 600 people, Nepali police reported on Saturday, as residents struggle to reconcile the mass scale of destruction left in their wake .

The devastation in Nepal is bringing back memories of the earthquake which took place in the country in April 2015 , when some of the same communities were hit by a similar disaster, a leading relief worker tells CNN.

Srijana Gurung, Nepal’s interim country director for Plan International said Saturday that “not once, but twice,” communities, children and young people are now facing “shock after shock,” with some of the hardest-hit areas once again difficult to reach.

Gurung expressed her grief over the devastation that took place when the flooding began, describing the scale of the destruction is “simply enormous” and nothing that anybody could comprehend.

The death toll from flash flooding in Nepal has climbed to 626, the country’s police said on Saturday.

So far, 2,301 people have been rescued, they added.

Officials in Nepal are planning to bury unidentifiable bodies in a mass grave as authorities struggle to cope with the decomposing remains.

An additional 7 people were confirmed dead in China today. Around 3,000 people are still missing both sides of the border.

Colossal flooding on the China-Nepal border on Wednesday was partly linked to the region’s steep terrain — a driver of landslides — and melting permafrost, an expert tells CNN.

As the long-frozen ground thaws, it weakens the slopes that are typically “glued together by ice-filled joints” along shattered bedrock near the surface, said Dr Richard Waller, author and senior lecturer in physical geography at the UK’s Keele University.

Officials raised concerns on Friday of a secondary flooding event with rain forecast in the area.

Damage from the original flood also raises the risk, with the area clogged with debris strewn in its wake, Dr Waller said.

“The original event will have deposited largely volumes of mud and rock along the course of its track,” he added.

“These accumulations will have blocked the rivers in tributary valleys such that lakes are now starting to form, posing the risk of follow up flood events.

“If this encourages the formation of a deep lake, then it could fail catastrophically and drain rapidly. There may, for example, be ice within the dam that could thaw and promote failure.”

In this event, the secondary flooding would likely be on a smaller scale, since both the lake and the amount of material involved are smaller, he added.

Residents in Nepal’s border region face widespread damage and mud-covered street after catastrophic flooding in the area earlier in the week.

Here are some of the latest images we’re seeing from Nepal.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal also warned that the bodies of those who died following Wednesday’s devastating flash flooding in Nepal are at risk of fast decomposition.

Speaking during today’s press conference, Khanal added that he had reached out to foreign governments asking them to provide freezers in order to keep people in a state of preservation, although he had so far not had any commitment on this.

He also highlighted some of the challenges search and rescue teams were facing with at least 3,000 people remain missing in the disaster.

Only helicopters can reach some of the areas hardest hit by flash flooding in Nepal, Khanal said, adding that they have to navigate their way through narrow gorges in some cases.

“Our Nepali helicopters have to stand in a queue just to get through those narrow gorges,” he said.

Nepal has sought help from neighbouring countries after deadly flash flooding, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has told a press conference, as search and rescue operations continue with at least 3,000 people missing.

The government has sought specific and specialized assistance from friendly neighboring countries, Khanal said.

This includes 11 personnel from India specialising in rescuing people who have become trapped in tunnels, the foreign minister said, while more of such personnel are expected to arrive in Nepal from China.

Chris Miller, the Culinary Director of World Central Kitchen, is no stranger to being on the ground when tragedy hits, but as catastrophic floods swept through villages along Nepal’s border with China, he said whole towns were gone, fast.

“What’s different about this is the speed in which this happened,” Miller told CNN’s Elex Michaelson from Kathmandu, roughly an hour to two hours south of where the devastation is. “Within 20, 30 minutes, the town was gone.”

World Central Kitchen is partnering with local restaurants in the area to provide hot meals for survivors, Miller added.

“We’re going to start setting up field kitchens with these organizations. They’re ready to cook,” he said, adding that the focus of the weekend was to reach hard-hit areas further north.

“Once we get those set up, we’ll just keep moving forward and keep moving forward and keep moving forward.”

A missing mechanical engineer uploaded a video of an emergency alert ringing through the hydro power plant where he worked in Nepal, just minutes before the torrent of floodwater hit on Wednesday.

Pratik Gautam, 26, was living and working at the Doosan camp, at the Upper Trishuli-1 project in Rasuwa, after graduating from Kathmandu University, his brother Prabhav Gautam told CNN.

At 9.06am on Wednesday, Pratik uploaded a short video to Snapchat in which sirens can be heard sounding at the camp and people are seen running in the courtyard on the mountainside.

Prabhav has not heard from his brother since and says the family are “losing hope” more than 72 hours after the disaster.

Pratik recorded the video outside, meaning he had left his office, but the family don’t know what happened next, Prabhav said.

“In another video, I saw a company boss and two small vehicles. I suspected that my brother and other engineers were in that vehicle but I’m not sure. Nobody in that vehicle was rescued or moved to a safe place.”

Prabhav said his brother had told him that there had been emergency signals at the camp warning of floods in the past.

“They used to climb up the hill or go to the high ground.”

Along a devastated main street, underneath downed power lines and past bundles of corn hung out to dry, Sadip Nepal stood outside the wrecked home he said he and his family had just managed to flee in time to save themselves.

Nepal was about to sit down to eat with his parents when he stepped outside onto a balcony and saw a torrent of water barreling into the village.

Inside the house, hardened mud two feet deep caked the ground floor and debris blocked the stairs. Flotsam from the deluge was scattered around: pieces of metal, rope, tree branches. Out in the back, two animal carcasses washed in by the river had begun to stink.

Nepal said there was “no chance” he could ever go back to live in the home he had been born in; there had been too much damage.

“We cannot do anything,” he said, holding back tears. “Now we have to start from zero.”

Seven people have been confirmed dead and 554 missing after the catastrophic flooding at Gyirong Port in Tibet, Chinese state media reported in an update Saturday.

Two villagers were also rescued, state media reported.

A police dog team was combing half-buried houses in the devastated town of Devighat on Saturday, looking for corpses.

Over the doorways filled with silt and debris, ornate signs carry the inhabitants’ family name or Hindu blessings, signs of the domesticity ruined when the nearby Trishuli river burst its banks in Nepal’s worst natural disaster in years.

A search team member poked a cane into the feet-deep silt to detect any sign of a body beneath it.

Nearby, the putrefied carcass of a buffalo lay by the road and its stench saturated the air.

The 14-member police team from the capital Kathmandu and their two dogs have been working from dawn til dusk for the past four days.

“It breaks my heart,” Krishna, one of the policemen, who did not want to give his last name, told CNN.

The last body police had pulled out was earlier this morning, of a young man. He was wearing blue jeans, Krishna said, but there was little else to identify him by. “His body had already decomposed,” Krishna said.

Tallying the dead and missing is laborious, Krishna the policeman said. Teams like his, deployed from other parts of the country, rely on the few locals still here for information on who is still missing and where they were last seen.

One policeman and a dog scrambled over debris into what once was a small shop to check the shop owner’s registration certificate fixed to the wall.

One man dug with a shovel trying to get into the ground floor to begin the long task of seeing if anything was salvageable. Others walked by carrying possessions; a microwave, a set of chairs and cooking pots.

Video from Xinhua shows rescuers attaching bags of supplies to drones for delivery to teams responding to catastrophic flooding in Tibet.

The amount of meltwater lost from glaciers in high-mountain Asia each year is enough to inundate the New York City island of Manhattan in over 1,200 feet of water, said Dan McGrath, associate professor in the department of geosciences at Colorado State University.

There are about 95,000 glaciers in the mountains of Asia, which cumulatively cover an area about the size of South Korea, McGrath told CNN’s John Berman on Friday.

“These glaciers are losing mass very rapidly,” McGrath said. “We’re looking at the top of the Empire State Building, submerged in water every single year from glaciers across the region.”

Wednesday’s disaster was caused by a glacial collapse which triggered a massive landslide and flooding .

Deadly flooding along the China-Nepal border has put a sharp spotlight on how risks from natural disasters in the Himalayas are growing, at the same time that countries in the region are rapidly building out their high-altitude infrastructure footprints.

There’s no indication that the latest disaster was linked to manmade development. But the devastation could be a reality check for governments driving a boom in dams, tunnels, highways, railways and bridges across the Himalayas as they aim to harness the region’s vast hydropower potential and resources –– and fortify their borders there.

No country has marshaled those efforts like China, where the government sees Tibet, and its Himalayan borderlands, as critical to its national and energy security.

Beijing aims to transform the region into a high-altitude green energy powerhouse, with projects that include a $168 billion megadam, currently under construction, that could stretch the limits of what human engineering has achieved.

And it’s not just China. India, and to a lesser extent Nepal, have been on an infrastructure-building spree in recent years, funneling hundreds of millions of dollars into developments in a part of the world that is acutely vulnerable to earthquakes, natural hazards and climate change.

Officials in the central Nepali district of Chitwan are planning to bury hundreds of unidentified bodies in a mass grave at a sacred Hindu site, local police told CNN.

Authorities are struggling to cope with the number of already decomposing bodies that have been recovered, with mortuaries at capacity. Out of 233 bodies recovered in Chitwan district, just four were able to be identified, said Ganesh Aryal, Chitwan’s chief district officer.

The bodies will be buried on the riverbank in Devghat, a Hindu pilgrimage town, beginning later today.

Before they are buried, DNA from the bodies will be collected so that they may be identified later, Aryal said.

Cremation is the preferred funeral rite in Hinduism. Aryal said the burial sites will be marked in the hopes that families will be able to locate the remains of their loved ones in the future.

A Nepali MP previously told CNN it has been a “major challenge” to identify bodies, which were badly disfigured and caked in mud following the tragic floods. Desperate families have been waiting outside hospitals searching for news about their loved ones.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said the government has requested foreign help for identifying and storing dead bodies, Reuters reported.

Sumnima Uddas, a Nepali Member of Parliament, gave an update to CNN on the massive emergency response to Wednesday’s devastating landslide near the border with China.

“Time is really of the essence to search and rescue as many survivors as we can,” Uddas told CNN’s Elex Michaelson.

More than 2,000 people in Nepal are still missing, including more than 500 foreign nationals, said Uddas, who is the chair of the International Relations & Tourism Parliamentary Committee and a former CNN international correspondent.

About 15,000 security personnel have been deployed to help with the emergency response. Nearly 4,500 people have been rescued so far. There are still about 900 people trapped in hydropower tunnels, she said.

Uddas added that identifying bodies has been “a major challenge.”

It’s Saturday morning in Nepal and the 72-hour “golden window” for finding survivors of a natural disaster is coming to a close. Anguished families are still seeking information on missing relatives after Wednesday’s catastrophic flooding near the China-Nepal border.

Death toll: 616 people have been killed in Nepal, according to police on Saturday. Around 2,500 people, including Americans and other foreigners, remain missing. In an update at Friday afternoon local time , Chinese state media reported that five people were confirmed dead, with more than 500 still missing.

Scenes of devastation: Chinese state media reported there is no sign of survivors at the border crossing which was engulfed by the flood wave. And in Nepal, health officials said residents of a “whole village that seems to have been washed away” are in “dire need of support.”

Flood concerns: Authorities are monitoring a second newly formed lake. Both the lake and another newly formed body of water sit upstream of an area where Wednesday’s catastrophic flash floods happened. A scientist said it could be “extremely concerning” if the second lake bursts it banks. More rain is also expected at the flood zone in Nepal over the weekend.

On the ground: A CNN team on the ground saw helicopters taking off from Trishuli barracks , the nerve center of rescue operations, from early Saturday local time. Meanwhile in Kathmandu, family members spent the night outside a hospital and put up posters with photos of their missing relatives, hoping to get information on their loved ones.

There is no sign of survivors at the Chinese border crossing which was engulfed by a ferocious flood wave earlier this week, rescue officials told state media.

Chinese rescuers arrived Friday afternoon at the land port, an area over 3,800 meters above sea level.

“The buildings within the mudslide’s impact zone have largely been flattened, with no discernible outline of any structures,” Liu Maolin, a rescue team leader, told state broadcaster CCTV.

“The ground is covered by thick layers of mud and rubble, with extensive and deep deposits, while the port’s infrastructure has been particularly severely damaged.”

So far, no survivors have been found, but the team “will never give up as long as there is even the slightest hope,” Liu said.

Carrying dozens of kilograms of equipment, the crew is battling extreme conditions where “even taking simple steps could trigger severe chest tightness, shortness of breath, dizziness and headaches,” China Emergency Management News reported.

articles.title: 'Gang of dacoits': Yogi Adityanath says Akhilesh must apologise for UP 'loot and extortion'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Saturday attacked the Samajwadi Party, calling it a \"gang of dacoits\" and accusing its lead.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Saturday attacked the Samajwadi Party, calling it a "gang of dacoits" and accusing its leadership of looting the state exchequer during its tenure.Speaking in Deoria, he said SP president Akhilesh Yadav should apologise to the people of Uttar Pradesh over the alleged financial irregularities linked to the construction of the Jayaprakash Narayan International Centre (JPNIC) in Lucknow.Adityanath made the remarks while laying the foundation stones for 80 development projects worth more than Rs 305 crore in Deoria. He also contrasted the current state government with previous administrations, claiming that Uttar Pradesh had moved away from an image associated with poor governance, insecurity and the influence of criminal networks."SP means loot and extortion, SP means a gang of dacoits," Adityanath said.He directly targeted Akhilesh Yadav over the alleged misuse of public funds, saying, "For the loot of the state exchequer that the SP chief committed for his indulgence, he should apologise to the people," he said, referring to alleged corruption in the construction of the Jayaprakash Narayan International Centre (JPNIC) in Lucknow.Adityanath says UP has left 'BIMARU' image behindThe chief minister said Uttar Pradesh had previously been dominated by what he described as a "parallel government of mafias". He claimed the situation had changed under his administration, with criminal networks being dismantled and the state's image improving."Now UP has a good image. Mafias have been reduced to dust. Those who breach the security of daughters and traders have only two places to go -- they are either in jail or in hell," Adityanath said.He also linked development and governance to the election of "good public representatives", saying that the state's progress was a result of the choices made by voters."When good public representatives are elected, good governments come and the results are also good. This development, prosperity and employment are the result of the hard work of the public representatives whom you elected," he said.The chief minister said Uttar Pradesh had faced a severe deficit in development and public services before 2017."Before 2017, there was neither development nor security nor respect in Uttar Pradesh. There was no employment, nor houses, toilets, LPG connections, electricity and roads for the poor. Schools had become centres of cheating," he said.CM attacks SP-Congress over encephalitis deathsAdityanath also revisited the issue of encephalitis, which he said had caused widespread fear in eastern Uttar Pradesh for decades. He identified Deoria, Maharajganj, Gorakhpur, Siddharthnagar, Kushinagar, Sant Kabir Nagar and Basti among the districts that were particularly affected between July 15 and November 15 each year."This was not a disease; it was the sick mentality of the SP-Congress governments. In 40 years, 50,000 innocent children died, but no chief minister or prime minister from the SP or the Congress came to take stock of the situation," Adityanath said.The chief minister also invoked the term 'BIMARU', which was coined by demographer Ashish Bose in the mid-1980s to describe Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, then among India's poorest states.Adityanath said Uttar Pradesh had now moved beyond that description, pointing to improvements in development, security and infrastructure as evidence of the state's transformation.Agriculture minister Surya Pratap Shahi, minister of state for rural development Vijay Lakshmi Gautam, and MLAs Shalabh Mani Tripathi and Sabha Kunwar Kushwaha were among those present at the Deoria programme.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: At least 27 dead after Russian drone attack triggers multiple blasts and fire at warehouse near Kyiv
articles.summary: At least 27 people have been killed and dozens wounded after a Russian drone attack triggered an explosion at a warehouse near Kyiv.
articles.body: At least 27 people have been killed and dozens wounded after a Russian drone attack triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted for hours at a warehouse in a residential area near Kyiv. The attack — in the Bucha district — came amid near constant aerial assaults from Russia but the likely storage of ammunition at the warehouse has had catastrophic consequences. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky vowed to punish those responsible. “Unfortunately, as of now, 27 people are known to have died. And this figure may not be final. I offer my sincere condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims,” said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv region military administration. Tkachenko said that more than 40 people were injured in the attack and more than 380 others, including dozens of children, had to be evacuated from the area. He said at least 50 residential buildings were damaged. Videos and photos shared by local residents show several completely destroyed buildings, with a little more than a few bare walls and scorched earth left. Russia’s defense ministry said its forces struck an arms depot storing drone making equipment. Speaking about the attack, Zelensky did not explicitly reveal the details of what kind of a warehouse was hit by the Russians, but said an investigation would be opened into the incident because “ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas.” Separately, the office of Ukraine’s Prosecutor General said in a statement that “explosive objects and materials” were stored in the premises and that an investigation would be opened into “the circumstances surrounding the explosion on the premises of the facility and the actions of the officials responsible.” Zelensky said a care home for elderly citizens and people living with disabilities was among the dozens of building damaged in the attack, and that more than 300 emergency services personnel were responding on the scene. Days of non-stop terror The deadly blast came as Kyiv has endured more than two days of near non-stop Russian attacks. According to a CNN tally, there have been 28 air raid alerts between midnight on Thursday and midday on Saturday, lasting more than 28 hours in total. While some missile strikes were recorded on Thursday, most of the attacks over the past few days were by jet-powered drones. These are a relatively new addition to Russia’s arsenal, having been first spotted around the start of the year. They can be exceptionally dangerous. Jet-powered drones fly at speeds of up to 500 kilometers per hour (310 miles per hour), evading Ukraine’s air defenses. They are also too fast for Kyiv’s mobile fire groups, so the only way to shoot them down is with ground-to-air missiles or fighter jets – both of which are in extremely limited supply in Ukraine. This story has been updated.

articles.title: Iran’s leaders acknowledge economic toll of war, pledge diplomacy, defence
articles.summary: Iran’s president said sanctions and the US naval blockade had caused exports and imports to slump by nearly 35 percent.
articles.body:
Iran’s leaders have acknowledged the mounting economic damage of six months of war with the United States , with the president saying foreign trade has shrunk by more than a third under US sanctions and a naval blockade.

The admissions came on Saturday as Tehran signalled it would not back down, pledging to withstand US pressure , pursue diplomacy and maintain what it says is control over the Strait of Hormuz.

The government said addressing the economic fallout was now a central focus, including curbing inflation, creating jobs and gradually reducing dependence on the dollar.

President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that exports and imports had slumped nearly 35 percent because of sanctions and the blockade of Iranian ports .

He said Iran had nonetheless managed to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the short-lived Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed with Washington in June, when oil sales were briefly permitted.

Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen publicly since the US and Israel launched the war on February 28 with an attack that killed his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, called on the government to tackle the hardship.

“There is the need to seriously address the chain of economic and livelihood challenges, ⁠such as inflation, unemployment, management of prices and the market for goods and services,” read a written statement attributed to Khamenei.

Annual inflation hit 66 percent last month, and residents in Tehran told Al Jazeera the war had upended daily life.

“Before the war, I didn’t work. Since the war, I’ve had to find a job to help support my household,” said Maryam. “Everything has become so expensive.”

Omid, who runs a food business, said trade had dried up as rents rose: “We can barely afford to pay our workers.”

In a statement on Saturday, the government described diplomacy and defence as “two complementary, coordinated and inseparable wings” for protecting national interests and territorial integrity, saying it would pursue both in a balanced manner.

Al Jazeera’s Sinem Koseoglu, reporting from Tehran, said the government was promoting a message of unity.

Pezeshkian has called for dialogue and a less confrontational relationship with neighbouring countries, saying none of them ruled over the other, while the supreme leader has urged domestic unity and the preservation of social cohesion, she said.

Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani met Iranian leaders in Tehran on Thursday, stressing the importance of returning to open shipping through the strait. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described the talks as “creative”.

Iran’s military, meanwhile, struck a defiant note, with army commander-in-chief Amir Hatami telling the Fars news agency that although the “enemy” had tried to destroy Iran’s drone and missile capabilities, its stockpile had been fired “with the utmost intensity until the last moment”.

On Friday, Acting Defence Minister Majid Ibn Reza said Iran had “surprises” in store: “Everyone, and especially the enemies, should know that they will become aware of Iran’s surprises in due time,” according to the Tasnim News Agency.

articles.title: ‘UP no longer Bimaru state’: CM Yogi says mafia crushed, encephalitis eradicated; Akhilesh flags gaps
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Saturday said the state had shed its image as a “Bimaru” state and now commanded a “respect.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Saturday said the state had shed its image as a “Bimaru” state and now commanded a “respectable image”, citing improvements in healthcare, connectivity, education and law and order.His remarks in Deoria came as Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav separately attacked the BJP government over the condition of the state's healthcare system, alleging shortages of doctors and paramedical staff.CM Yogi targets previous governmentsAddressing a programme in Deoria, where he inaugurated and laid the foundation stones for 80 development projects worth Rs 305 crore, Yogi accused previous Samajwadi Party and Congress governments of remaining indifferent to encephalitis deaths.“Encephalitis was not merely a disease; it was a sick mindset. It was the sick mentality of the Samajwadi Party and Congress governments of that time -- a mentality that was devouring the innocent lives here while the authorities remained completely indifferent,” Adityanath said, according to news agency ANI.He claimed that more than 50,000 innocent lives were lost over four decades and alleged that no chief minister from the Samajwadi Party or Congress, or Congress prime minister, had visited the region to assess the situation.Adityanath also alleged that a parallel “mafia rule” had operated across Uttar Pradesh under previous governments.“A parallel mafia rule operated across the state. Today, I can say that UP has truly lived up to its name. No one calls UP a 'Bimaru' state anymore. No one questions Uttar Pradesh now. The state now commands a respectable image,” he said.“The mafia has been crushed, wiped out completely. For those who threaten the safety of daughters and traders, there are only two places: either jail or hell; there is no third option,” he added.The chief minister said the government had moved from “one district, one mafia” to “one district, one medical college”, pointing to medical colleges in Deoria and Kushinagar.Deoria development projects, education and connectivityAdityanath said encephalitis had been eradicated and linked the development to the government's healthcare initiatives.He highlighted the medical college in Deoria named after Maharishi Deoraha Baba and said connectivity in the district was being improved through new bypasses and flyovers.“Single-lane roads are being converted to double lanes, double-lane roads to 4-lanes, and 4-lane roads to 6-lanes,” he said.The chief minister also highlighted composite schools, the upgradation of Kasturba Gandhi schools, Abhyudaya coaching facilities for competitive examinations and the transformation of basic education schools under the government's ‘Operation Kayakalp’ programme.Akhilesh alleges shortages in healthcare systemSeparately, Akhilesh Yadav alleged that Uttar Pradesh was facing shortages of doctors and paramedical staff and promised free treatment and medicines for poor people if the Samajwadi Party returned to power.Yadav claimed there was one doctor for every 16,000 people in the state and alleged that 41% of posts in government hospitals were vacant.“More than 24,000 posts in nursing and paramedical services are vacant,” he said.The former chief minister also claimed that 604 posts were vacant at AIIMS Gorakhpur and 579 at AIIMS Rae Bareli.He alleged that the number of primary health centres had declined in several districts, including Gorakhpur.“When the chief minister is reducing the number of health centres in his own district, imagine what the situation would be elsewhere,” Yadav said.Yadav further alleged that patients were being forced to spend heavily on treatment and medicines.“In the future, when the Samajwadi government is formed, no card will be asked for. A patient will come, and his treatment and medicines will be free,” he said.He said the proposal would cover routine as well as serious illnesses, including cancer, and would be included in the party's manifesto.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Russian attack on warehouse near Ukraine’s Kyiv kills at least 27
articles.summary: Zelenskyy says a warehouse was struck outside Kyiv, ‘followed by a detonation’, triggering a major fire and explosions.
articles.body:
At least 27 people have been killed after an overnight Russian attack on a warehouse in the Bucha district, outside the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, officials said.

“Unfortunately, as things stand, 27 people are known to have died. And this figure may not be final,” Kyiv regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Saturday. Among the dead was Taras Didych, mayor of the village of Dmytrivska, Tkachenko said.

A Russian drone struck a warehouse near Kyiv’s western suburbs storing munitions, sparking huge explosions, authorities said on Saturday.

Tymur Tkachenko, head of the local regional military administration, said that at least 50 residential buildings had been damaged in the attack, which caused a large-scale fire that spread to homes and a restaurant.

The warehouse appeared to have been storing “explosive objects”, according to Ukrainian prosecutors, who said they are opening an investigation into criminal negligence. The prosecutor’s office specified that its investigation would focus on “the legality of the storage of explosive objects and materials on the enterprise’s grounds”, as well as whether the company responsible, which was not named, had the “necessary permits and approvals”.

In a statement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a warehouse had been struck in the village of Myla “followed by a detonation”. He did not give details about the site, but confirmed that criminal proceedings would follow. “There are regulations in place – ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas,” Zelenskyy said.

Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, sparking fires and causing civilian casualties to soar.

Writing on the Telegram messaging app, Kyiv’s regional governor said that 42 people ⁠were injured and that ⁠more than ⁠380 others were ⁠being evacuated from the strike area ‌in the Bucha district.

Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi expressed regret that a “lesson” had not been learned after a previous deadly attack in July in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, on a munitions depot. That investigation revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company, which did not comply with standards to store ammunition well away from residential buildings.

“In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence,” Koretskyi said on Telegram. “Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations never happen again.”

Russia launched at least two missiles and 267 drones at Ukraine between late Friday and early Saturday, according to the Ukrainian Air Force.

In addition to the warehouse strike, Russian attacks early on Saturday killed one person in the southern Odesa region and a 14-year-old girl in the Kyiv suburb of Boryspil, regional officials said.

In Russia, at least three people were killed and ⁠nine wounded in a Ukrainian ‌drone attack in the Belgorod region, local authorities ⁠said on Telegram. Three of ⁠the injured ⁠are in serious condition, authorities added.

Another person was killed and three ⁠others were injured in a ‌Ukrainian drone attack in Russian-annexed Sevastopol, on the ⁠Crimean Peninsula, ⁠Mikhail Razvozhayev, the city’s ⁠Russian-appointed governor, ⁠said ⁠on Telegram.

Russia and Ukraine have for several months been intensifying their long-range strikes, increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure such as logistics warehouses and oil and port facilities, with these attacks causing a growing number of civilian casualties.

articles.title: The Italian pastry that’s caused a frenzy
articles.summary: This week in travel: An alpine hut packed with Italian pastries sparks a frenzy, a college town serves up serious pizza, and the younger Brits shunning pubs.
articles.body: This week in travel news: A frenzy erupts over Italian pastries, a college town serves up serious pizza, plus younger Brits are shunning the traditional night at the pub. Buon appetito! Known for its sumptuous cuisine and delicious desserts, Italy has tourists lining up for gelato all over the peninsula. But what about an Italian treat that’s sometimes overlooked – the pastry? Well, some travelers have put one particular doughy delight at the center of their itineraries, much to the chagrin of unassuming locals. A hiking hut in a peaceful, remote area of the Italian Dolomites has been overrun by visitors seeking out a pastry known locally as a krapfen or bombolone, a filled delicacy similar to a donut without a hole. Following the advice of food bloggers and influencers, overzealous visitors have thronged a rifugio (refuge) in Italy’s Val di Fassa valley, all because of this traditional pastry. Stanley Tucci also sampled pastries – without causing offense – during an episode of CNN’s “Searching for Italy.” US-based subscribers can stream the show here. South Korea’s first foreign haenyeo Can you imagine diving into the sea without breathing gear to catch fresh seafood? It’s likely few of us could, but it’s a tradition on Jeju Island in South Korea, where now an American woman has become the first foreigner to hold a license to be a haenyeo — the local term for female divers. Kylie Genter is a true rarity. “As a foreigner doing this, especially as a person who is not a Korean citizen, it’s a big responsibility,” she tells CNN. Genter lives in Youngrak-ri, a small coastal village on the far western side of Jeju Island. Most villages have their own groups of haenyeo. And their bond is strong: They eat, dive, bathe and relax together — while also keeping each other safe. CNN subscribers can read all about Genter and the haenyeo tradition here. No olive branch for Canada Amid another trade battle with Canada, President Trump issued an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America. The announcement is spurring fears of a fresh wave of Canadian travelers steering clear of the US. This past year, CNN Travel visited a stretch of the Florida coast known as “Little Quebec,” which was seeing a major dip in tourism because of the tariffs and political infighting between the two North American neighbors. We’ve also spoken with many Canadian snowbirds who opted for other destinations over the winter. A cultural oasis in New England Continuing our countdown of America’s Best Towns to Visit in 2026, we have New Haven at No. 2. New Haven is both a typical New England town dating from the colonial era – laid out in a grid with a historic town green – and also the chic, dynamic global home of Yale University. Connecticut’s cultural capital, New Haven is an urban walker’s paradise, abounding in good eats and history. Spend time with master art works by Rodin, Van Gogh and Turner – for free – and then grab a coffee or enjoy your pick of historic hamburger joints, food trucks, taco places and Ethiopian restaurants. Another thing that’s put the Connecticut city on the map? Pizza. To paraphrase Yalie and Revolutionary War hero Nathan Hale, you may regret that you have but one weekend to give to New Haven. Take a look, too, at the rest of our list so far: Roanoke, Virginia, at No. 10; Lawrence, Kansas, at No. 9; Iowa City, Iowa at No. 8; Juneau, Alaska, at No. 7; Burlington, Vermont, at No. 6; Fort Collins, Colorado, at No. 5; Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, at No. 4; and Greenville, South Carolina at No. 3. Next week, we’ll tell you all about our No. 1 pick. Do you have a suggestion for the 2027 list? Tell us about it here. In case you missed it Britain’s Gen Z is shunning the traditional night at the pub. These young people are just as likely to head to the running track after work. A man called the “Beast Runner” searches Taiwan’s mountains for missing hikers. He follows clues even after everyone else has given up. A restaurant in Bangkok says food first, not phones. Run by a celebrity chef, it invites diners to enjoy the meal without a screen. A legend remembered. A measles surge. A tragic flood. What do you remember from the week that was?
